১৯) For the diagnosis of primary pulmonary tuberculosis in children, who often do not expectorate sputum, specimen for culture can be obtained from?
Medicine-10.exp:
Young children with primary pulmonary tuberculosis usually swallow their sputum instead of expectorating it. Therefore, early-morning gastric lavage (gastric aspirate) is collected to recover swallowed Mycobacterium tuberculosis for:

  • Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear

  • Culture

  • Nucleic acid amplification tests (e.g., GeneXpert MTB/RIF)

The specimen is collected early in the morning before eating, when swallowed respiratory secretions have accumulated in the stomach overnight.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Nasal secretion — Not a standard specimen for diagnosing pulmonary TB.

  • B. Throat swab — Poor diagnostic yield for pulmonary TB.

  • C. Early-morning gastric lavage — Correct. Standard specimen in children who cannot produce sputum.

  • D. Faeces — Not routinely used for culture in the diagnosis of pulmonary TB.

High-yield Recall

Patient Preferred Specimen
Adult with productive cough Sputum
Child unable to expectorate Early-morning gastric lavage (gastric aspirate)
Alternative in children Induced sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage (selected cases)
Common MCQ trap Children swallow sputum → Gastric aspirate for TB diagnosis

Exam pearl: Early-morning gastric lavage is the specimen of choice for microbiological diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis in young children who cannot expectorate sputum.

Medicine-10.question: ২০) Leptospira interrogans persist indefinitely in
Medicine-10.exp:
Leptospira interrogans persists in the renal proximal convoluted tubules of infected humans and animals. From there, the organisms are shed in the urine for prolonged periods, serving as an important source of transmission.

This renal colonization explains why urine becomes positive during the immune phase of leptospirosis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Mucous membrane — Entry site of infection, not the site of persistent colonization.

  • B. Bowman's capsule — Not the site where Leptospira persists.

  • C. Juxtaglomerular apparatus — Not involved in persistent infection.

  • D. Convoluted tubules of the kidney — Correct. Organisms persist in the proximal renal tubules and are excreted in urine.

High-yield Recall

Feature Key Point
Causative organism Leptospira interrogans
Reservoir Rats, dogs, cattle and other mammals
Mode of transmission Contact with urine-contaminated water or soil
Site of persistence Proximal convoluted tubules of the kidney
Severe disease Weil's disease (jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage)
Common MCQ trap Leptospira persists in renal tubules → prolonged urinary shedding

Exam pearl: Leptospira can be isolated from blood during the first week of illness and from urine during the later (immune) phase because it persists in the renal tubules.

Medicine-10.question: ২১) Campylobacter jejuni infection have been linked to
Medicine-10.exp:
Campylobacter jejuni is the most common antecedent bacterial infection associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). The mechanism is molecular mimicry: antibodies formed against the bacterial lipooligosaccharides (LOS) cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides, leading to acute immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy.

GBS typically develops 1–3 weeks after the diarrheal illness.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Gas gangrene — Caused by Clostridium perfringens.

  • B. Myocarditis — More commonly associated with viruses (e.g., Coxsackie B virus).

  • C. Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) — Correct. Classical post-infectious complication of Campylobacter jejuni.

  • D. Inflammatory bowel disease — Campylobacter causes acute gastroenteritis; it is not a classical cause of IBD.

High-yield Recall

Organism Important Association
Campylobacter jejuni Guillain–Barré syndrome, Reactive arthritis
Clostridium perfringens Gas gangrene
Coxsackie B virus Myocarditis
Yersinia enterocolitica Reactive arthritis, erythema nodosum
Common MCQ trap Campylobacter → GBS via molecular mimicry

Exam pearl: Among infectious agents, Campylobacter jejuni is the most common antecedent infection associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome.

Medicine-10.question: ২২) Mycobacterium leprae has tropism for
Medicine-10.exp:
Mycobacterium leprae has a predilection (tropism) for Schwann cells of the peripheral nervous system and macrophages in the skin. Infection of Schwann cells leads to:

  • Peripheral neuropathy

  • Loss of sensation

  • Muscle weakness

  • Nerve thickening

  • Deformities in advanced disease

The organism grows best at cooler temperatures (27–33°C), explaining its preference for the skin, peripheral nerves, ears, nose, and testes.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Extraglomerular mesangial cells — Not a target of M. leprae.

  • B. Schwann cells — Correct. Principal site of infection in peripheral nerves.

  • C. Upper respiratory mucosae — Important portal of entry and transmission, but not the characteristic site of tropism.

  • D. Testes — May be involved in advanced lepromatous leprosy but are not the primary target.

High-yield Recall

Feature Key Point
Causative organism Mycobacterium leprae
Characteristic tropism Schwann cells of peripheral nerves
Preferred temperature 27–33°C (cool body sites)
Major clinical feature Peripheral neuropathy with sensory loss
Commonly affected sites Skin, peripheral nerves, ears, nose, testes
Common MCQ trap Schwann cell invasion is the hallmark of leprosy

Exam pearl: The hallmark of leprosy is infection of Schwann cells, leading to anesthetic skin lesions and thickened peripheral nerves.

Medicine-10.question: ২৩) Only notable physical signs in leptospirosis
Medicine-10.exp:
Conjunctival congestion (conjunctival suffusion) is the characteristic and often the only notable physical sign of leptospirosis. It is highly suggestive of the disease and occurs without purulent discharge, helping to distinguish it from bacterial conjunctivitis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Macular rash — Uncommon and not a characteristic sign.

  • B. Hepatomegaly — May occur in severe disease (Weil's disease) but is not the only notable physical sign.

  • C. Conjunctival congestion — Correct. Classical physical sign of leptospirosis.

  • D. Epistaxis — May occur due to hemorrhagic complications but is not the characteristic physical sign.

High-yield Recall

Feature Key Point
Causative organism Leptospira interrogans
Characteristic physical sign Conjunctival suffusion (congestion)
Transmission Contact with urine-contaminated water or soil
Severe form Weil's disease (jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage)
Common MCQ trap Conjunctival suffusion is a classic clue to leptospirosis

Exam pearl: Think of leptospirosis in a patient with fever, myalgia (especially calf tenderness), and conjunctival suffusion after exposure to contaminated water.

Medicine-10.question: ২৪) Highest eosinophil counts found in
Medicine-10.exp:
Strongyloides stercoralis infection is classically associated with marked eosinophilia, especially during larval tissue migration. Among the listed helminthic infections, strongyloidiasis typically produces the highest eosinophil counts.

Note: In disseminated (hyperinfection) strongyloidiasis, eosinophilia may be absent despite severe disease.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Cestode infections — Usually cause minimal or mild eosinophilia, unless there is tissue invasion (e.g., cysticercosis).

  • B. Ascariasis — Causes eosinophilia during the lung migration phase, but generally less marked.

  • C. Filariasis — Causes eosinophilia, particularly in tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, but not typically as high as strongyloidiasis in standard MCQs.

  • D. Strongyloidiasis — Correct. Characteristically associated with marked eosinophilia.

High-yield Recall

Infection Eosinophilia
Strongyloidiasis Marked (highest among these options)
Filariasis Marked
Ascariasis Moderate (during larval migration)
Cestode infections Mild or absent unless tissue invasion
Common MCQ trap Tissue-invasive helminths produce the greatest eosinophilia.

Exam pearl: The degree of eosinophilia correlates with tissue migration of helminth larvae rather than the presence of adult worms in the intestinal lumen.

Medicine-10.question: ২৫) After swimming in a river a patient developed itching & hematuria . What is the most important treatment for him ?
Medicine-10.exp:
A patient who develops itching after swimming in a river followed by hematuria is highly suggestive of urinary schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium.

Typical features include:

  • Cercarial dermatitis ("swimmer's itch") after freshwater exposure

  • Terminal hematuria

  • Dysuria

  • Chronic infection may lead to bladder fibrosis, hydronephrosis, and squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder

Praziquantel is the drug of choice for all major forms of schistosomiasis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Mebendazole — Effective against many intestinal nematodes, not schistosomiasis.

  • B. Praziquantel — Correct. First-line treatment for Schistosoma infection.

  • C. Ivermectin — Used for strongyloidiasis and onchocerciasis, not schistosomiasis.

  • D. Albendazole — Used for many nematode infections and hydatid disease, not the treatment of choice for schistosomiasis.

High-yield Recall

Parasite Characteristic Feature Drug of Choice
Schistosoma haematobium Hematuria, urinary schistosomiasis Praziquantel
Schistosoma mansoni Intestinal/hepatic schistosomiasis Praziquantel
Strongyloides stercoralis Larva currens Ivermectin
Ascaris lumbricoides Intestinal obstruction Albendazole
Common MCQ trap Freshwater exposure + hematuria = S. haematobium → Praziquantel

Exam pearl: Painless terminal hematuria in a person with freshwater exposure is a classic presentation of Schistosoma haematobium infection; treat with praziquantel.

Medicine-10.question: ২৬) Most commonly used investigations for detection of toxoplasmosis
Medicine-10.exp:
The Sabin–Feldman dye test is the classical reference (gold standard) serological test for the detection of toxoplasmosis by demonstrating antibodies against Toxoplasma gondii.

Although PCR is widely used today—especially for congenital toxoplasmosis, amniotic fluid, and CNS disease—the traditional single best answer in microbiology MCQs is Sabin–Feldman dye test.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. MRI — Useful for detecting brain lesions in cerebral toxoplasmosis but not for confirming the infection.

  • B. PCR — Highly sensitive and widely used in specific clinical settings, but classically not the standard MCQ answer for routine detection.

  • C. CSF IgM antibody test — Not routinely used for diagnosis.

  • D. Sabin–Feldman dye test — Correct. Classical reference test for toxoplasmosis.

High-yield Recall

Test Role
Sabin–Feldman dye test Classical gold standard serological test
PCR Congenital infection, amniotic fluid, CNS toxoplasmosis
IgM antibody Recent/acute infection
IgG antibody Past exposure or immunity
Common MCQ trap Classical answer = Sabin–Feldman dye test; Modern practice = PCR in selected cases

Exam pearl: For traditional MBBS/FCPS microbiology MCQs, the expected answer is Sabin–Feldman dye test, whereas PCR has become increasingly important in current clinical practice.

২৮) 1st sign of infection in kala azar
Medicine-10.exp:
The earliest clinical manifestation of Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is usually an insidious low-grade fever, which gradually becomes high-grade, irregular, and prolonged as the disease progresses.

Other features such as splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, anemia, weight loss, and black pigmentation develop later.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Low-grade fever — Correct. Usually the first sign of infection.

  • B. High-grade fever — Develops later as the disease progresses.

  • C. Splenomegaly — Characteristic finding but not the earliest sign.

  • D. Black pigmentation — Occurs in chronic disease and gives rise to the name Kala-azar ("black fever").

High-yield Recall

Feature Key Point
Causative organism Leishmania donovani
Vector Female sandfly (Phlebotomus)
First sign Low-grade fever
Most characteristic sign Massive splenomegaly
Classical late features Fever, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, skin hyperpigmentation
Common MCQ trap First sign = Low-grade fever; Most characteristic sign = Massive splenomegaly

Exam pearl: In visceral leishmaniasis, fever precedes organomegaly. Massive splenomegaly is the hallmark finding, but the earliest manifestation is a low-grade fever.

৩৯) “Break-bone fever” is suggestive of?
Medicine-10.exp:
"Break-bone fever" is the classic nickname for dengue fever because of the severe muscle, bone, and joint pains experienced by patients. It is caused by the dengue virus (a Flavivirus) and transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Lyme disease — Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi; characterized by erythema migrans and arthritis.

  • B. Relapsing fever — Caused by Borrelia species; presents with recurrent episodes of fever.

  • C. Typhoid fever — Caused by Salmonella Typhi; presents with prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms, and rose spots.

  • D. Dengue fever — Correct. Known as "break-bone fever" because of severe musculoskeletal pain.

High-yield Recall

Disease Characteristic Feature
Dengue fever Break-bone fever, severe myalgia and arthralgia
Lyme disease Erythema migrans (bull's-eye rash)
Relapsing fever Recurrent febrile episodes
Typhoid fever Step-ladder fever, rose spots

Exam pearl: Think: Dengue = Break-bone fever + Retro-orbital pain + Severe myalgia + Aedes mosquito.

Medicine-10.question: ৪০) Which of the following is the commonest physical finding in enteric fever?
Medicine-10.exp:
In enteric (typhoid) fever, the commonest physical finding is a coated tongue, typically with a dirty white coating in the center and red margins and tip ("typhoid tongue").

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Coated tongue — Correct. Most common physical finding.

  • B. Abdominal tenderness — May occur but is less common and less characteristic.

  • C. Rose spots — Classical but seen in only a minority of patients.

  • D. Hepatosplenomegaly — May be present, especially splenomegaly, but is not the commonest physical finding.

High-yield Recall

Feature Key Point
Causative organism Salmonella Typhi
Commonest physical finding Coated (typhoid) tongue
Characteristic rash Rose spots (uncommon)
Common abdominal findings Hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal tenderness
Common MCQ trap Rose spots are classical but not the commonest finding.

Exam pearl: Typhoid fever: coated tongue + step-ladder fever + relative bradycardia (Faget sign) + abdominal symptoms are classic examination clues.
